title: Lecture 1. Health and Illness in Psychology
summary:
📋 Main Topics of the Lecture
  1. Health and Illness in Psychology
  2. The Problem of Defining Health
  3. What is Illness
  4. Prerequisites for the Creation of the Biomedical Model of Illness
  5. The Biomedical Model of Illness
  6. Prerequisites for the Creation of the Model of Non-communicable (Chronic) Diseases
  7. Holistic Model of Health and Non-communicable (Chronic) Diseases
  8. Some Conclusions in the Context of Prevention

1. The Problem of Defining Health The Constitution of the World Health Organization (1948): Human health is a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease and infirmity.

This definition clearly demonstrates the lack of a unified approach to understanding health. Healthy behavior is such a difficult and complex phenomenon to define that there is no empirical confirmation of its existence in science. If we try to imagine an absolutely healthy person, it is unlikely that we will succeed. Even the (completely impossible) full compliance of our hypothetical person's behavior with medical and social norms leaves open the question of their psychological well-being, which is difficult to objectively assess. Ultimately, when assessing health, we will be forced to rely on the individual's subjective assessment, or, more simply, on whether the person themselves feels healthy and happy?

Thus, even superficial reflections on the phenomenon of health lead us to the following possible approaches to its understanding:

Medical objective assessment of the condition, expressed in the absence of clinical symptoms and psychiatric or somatic diagnosis, compliance with medical norms (biomedical approach). Subjective assessment of one's physical and/or mental state, integrally expressed in self-assessment of health, life satisfaction, and a sense of subjective happiness. It is important to note that a person, when characterizing their somatic well-being, inevitably speaks not about "objective" health, but its reflection in the psyche, which is subject to complex psychological regularities, due to which the "gap" between "objective" and "subjective" health can be very large. From this, it follows that this "gap" is the subject of analysis for psychology (subjective socio-psychological approach). Human adaptation to the social environment, successful functioning in society, adaptation to social institutions and organizations, which may include self-assessment indicators, as well as objective assessments of social well-being by other people (objective socio-psychological approach). These three approaches are represented in domestic and Western literature by numerous models (empirically verified in hundreds of studies). A significant body of specialized literature, from the 1960s to the present, has been devoted to the discussion and critique of these approaches, which can be summarized in the following provisions (Gurvich, 1999, pp. 16-21):

The main criticism regarding the medical assessment of health is that the absence of symptoms and diagnosis does not mean the absence of illness, which is well reflected by the well-known medical joke: "there are no healthy people, only under-examined ones."

Criticism regarding how a person assesses their somatic state is related to possible significant discrepancies between the results of objective and subjective health assessments. In particular, with the phenomenon of the so-called "positive illusion" in self-perception and perception of the environment. This phenomenon was discovered and confirmed by numerous studies, which revealed that most people have positive illusions in three directions: (a) they evaluate themselves in unrealistically positive terms; (b) they are convinced that they have greater control over their environment than they actually do; (c) they view their future more positively than baseline data would suggest. As an inverse effect, one can recall a mental disorder such as hypochondria, which consists of a person detecting various symptoms of somatic diseases in themselves that are not confirmed by doctors (which leads the hypochondriac to suspect diseases so serious that even doctors cannot detect them).

Criticism regarding models based on the idea of human adaptation to the social environment is that they were all developed within the ethical system of mid-20th century American culture, meaning they are culturally specific and do not account for cases of healthy adaptation to an unhealthy social environment. As examples, the authors cited a mentally healthy Nazi in Nazi society or well-adapted members of destructive cults.

And perhaps the main drawback of the approaches mentioned above is that they do not offer a unified theoretical framework for describing the concepts of health and illness and do not resolve the contradiction between medical and socio-psychological explanations of health, which, as we noted at the very beginning of the lesson, is contained in the WHO constitution's definition since 1948.

Looking ahead, it can be said that the noted contradiction has not yet been overcome. However, significant work has been done in this direction over the past half-century, which will be discussed in the next lesson, dedicated to defining the concept of illness.

2. What is Illness Illness, like health, is also one of the most complex and difficult concepts to define when it comes to humans. The traditional view of health, due to the difficulty of its definition, boils down to a negative definition, i.e., the absence of signs of illness. But over the last 100 years, the scientific understanding of illness has been significantly re-evaluated due to sharp changes in the structure of morbidity and causes of mortality in developed countries.

Throughout human history, the most common cause of mortality was infectious diseases and associated acute conditions. But after the invention of antibiotics at the turn of the 19th-20th centuries, against the backdrop of urbanization, rising well-being, and increased life expectancy for most of the population in developed countries, the nature of morbidity and causes of mortality began to change. Diseases known as non-communicable or chronic diseases gained predominant prevalence, and today they have become the main cause of death and disability worldwide. These primarily include cardiovascular diseases (such as heart attack and stroke), oncological diseases, chronic respiratory diseases (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma), and diabetes. Therefore, traditional ideas about health and illness had to be re-evaluated: biomedical theories had to be significantly supplemented with psychological and sociological models*.

  • It should be clarified that the line between infectious and chronic diseases is conditional: chronic diseases have acute phases, and infectious diseases can become chronic. Behavioral and lifestyle characteristics influence the onset, course, and outcome of infectious diseases, and even injuries. And past infections can influence lifestyle. But these details are beyond the scope of this course.

Let's turn to the data from Our World in Data: Causes of Death (https://ourworldindata.org/causes-of-death). ↗ You can follow the link. There is a function where if you move the slider from 1980 to 2023, the distribution of causes of death changes before your eyes: a large blue zone (chronic diseases) against small red (infections) and green (injuries) zones.

From these two cross-sections in the mortality structure, we can see the dynamics of a process that began 100 years ago – people are increasingly dying from non-communicable diseases and less from infectious ones. And if we sample developed countries, the trend becomes much more obvious. On the website https://ourworldindata.org/causes-of-death ↗ there is an interactive map of causes of death worldwide. Moving the slider through the years from 1980 to 2023, one can see how in just 40 years, the proportion of deaths from chronic diseases in the overall structure increased from 50 to 75%. And this indicates that in 40 years, the world has become 2.5 times more civilized, despite all the current chaos. Once upon a time, people simply did not live long enough to develop chronic diseases. And 100-150 years ago, thanks to urbanization, industrialization, and consequently, the development of healthcare systems, as well as the discovery of antibiotics, deaths from infections and acute conditions began to recede into the past

Reasons for the change in mortality structure in the 20th century:

urbanization (improved quality of life), development of the healthcare system, transition from traditional to industrial society, discovery of antibiotics (1928 A. Fleming, penicillin), increase in average life expectancy (from 35 to 70 years). Therefore, over the last hundred years, various scientific disciplines concerning health, human behavior, and society have developed particularly rapidly, integrating today into the general concept of Public Health, where health psychology occupies a central place:

The overwhelming volume of publications in psychological scientific journals today is, in one way or another, dedicated to health psychology. Several major psychological journals are dedicated to health psychology, such as "Health Psychology," "The Journal of Health Psychology," "The British Journal of Health Psychology," "Applied Psychology: Health and Well-Being," and others. A course in health psychology is part of the educational standard for psychologists in all universities worldwide. This is not by chance, but because the professional tasks that psychologists solve in almost any workplace can only be understood and implemented within the theoretical framework and using the tools of health psychology. 3. Prerequisites for the Creation of the Biomedical Model of Illness Mechanistic model of the organism: a human is, first and foremost, a body (machine), and illness is a breakdown of some part of it.

Cell theory: cells are the structural units of organisms (Robert Hooke, 1665), Rudolf Virchow: "Where there is a cell, there must have been a pre-existing cell" (1858).

Concept of specificity: the presence of specific pathogenic agents for each disease (L. Pasteur, 1880s).

Discovery of antibiotics: An antibiotic is a substance of microbial, animal, or plant origin capable of inhibiting the growth of certain microorganisms or causing their death (1928 A. Fleming, penicillin).

4. The Biomedical Model of Illness The biomedical model, originally intended to describe infectious diseases, includes:

a) the carrier of infection (host) – a specific person or group of specific people;

b) the infection itself (infectious agent): the cause of the disease is a specific pathogen – something material – a bacterium or virus that we can see under a microscope;

c) the environment – the entire spectrum of environmental factors determining the outcome of the interaction between the host and the infectious agent. In this case, biological, not behavioral, factors are primarily meant!

The model defines illness through the "battle" of the host, agent, and environment, and deviations from the norm of measurable biological (somatic) variables, which leaves no room for behavioral aspects of illness. Simply put, the biomedical model of illness is based on the assertion that a person became ill because they were accidentally infected. It does not matter how the person behaved. However, this model proved insufficient for describing chronic diseases.

5. Prerequisites for the Creation of the Model of Non-communicable (Chronic) Diseases Firstly, non-communicable diseases, such as cardiovascular diseases, arise without the involvement of any specific pathogen and develop gradually, possibly over years and decades. Unlike infectious diseases, where a person can become infected instantly, problems with the cardiovascular system can develop quite slowly against a background of prolonged stress, increased irritability, or low mood. Such a person is not considered entirely healthy, but from a medical point of view, there is nothing to treat yet, as there are no obvious symptoms of illness.

Secondly, the prevalence of non-communicable diseases follows certain social patterns. Infectious diseases spread more or less randomly: a person sneezed on a bus, and whoever was nearby got sick. Non-communicable diseases, however, spread among people who share certain behavioral traits or living conditions. For example, the fact that educators are more prone to cardiovascular diseases compared to representatives of other professions implies that the disease is not transmitted from person to person along with its pathogen, but is the result of chronic emotional stress characteristic of this professional group.

Therefore, carriers of chronic diseases are no longer just specific individuals, but primarily social groups. The main mechanism determining the similarity of health indicators among representatives of stable social groups (and consequently the difference from representatives of other groups) is the commonality of living conditions, subcultural features, and determinants of health-related individual behavior (health values; social attitudes towards medical care; group norms regulating health behavior). Therefore, a person's belonging to certain social groups often allows for a significantly more accurate prediction of their health risks than their constitutional-biological or personality-characterological characteristics.

Thirdly, due to non-specificity – unlike infectious diseases, where a certain infection can cause only one corresponding disease, for example, the influenza virus can only cause influenza, a chronic disease can be the result of a combination of various factors:

biological (e.g., viruses, bacteria, heredity); psychological (personality traits, presence of sources of chronic stress and ability to cope with them); social (behavioral norms, family, reference groups, work, social class affiliation, etc.). And on the other hand, the listed factors can lead to a wide variety of chronic diseases.

Fourthly, and most importantly!, human behavior plays a crucial role in the formation and course of non-communicable diseases. Here, the patient is no longer a passive participant in the process, to whom the doctor prescribes medications, as in the case of an infectious disease. For the development of the disease and its overcoming, it is important what lifestyle a person has, what beliefs they hold about their health, how strongly they want to recover, etc. From this arises the question of responsibility: in the case of an infectious disease, the patient is a passive victim, while in the case of a non-communicable disease, responsibility for recovery, to one degree or another, lies with the patient. Moreover, in psychotherapy, it is precisely the client's awareness of their responsibility for the emergence of their problem that is the starting point for overcoming it and regaining control over their life.

Simply put, the model of non-communicable disease is based on the assertion that a person became ill because they behaved accordingly. Therefore, treating such diseases requires not only and not so much pills and surgeries, but rather correcting the behavior and lifestyle that led to the disease.

The above-mentioned reasons led to the need to formulate a new positive concept of health that would not be limited solely to the absence of symptoms of any disease. Throughout the 20th century, behavioral sciences made many attempts to understand health through the presence of certain systemic properties that determine human well-being, not only at the level of the physical body, but also at the level of the person as an individual, at the level of social institutions and organizations in which the person is included, and at the level of the community in which they live.

The development of health concepts was largely associated with the functional approach of American sociologist Talcott Parsons, who understood health as a person's ability to fully function in major social roles, which implies a number of important consequences:

  • There is no "absolute" mental health. In other words, there is no person who could maintain health in all social roles or situations.
  • The concept of health depends on the socio-cultural norms of society. What is perceived as health in one culture may appear as severe pathology in another, and vice versa.
  • A functional understanding of health does not imply a complete absence of symptoms of a mental or somatic disorder, but only states that such symptomatology, if present, does not cause social or behavioral dysfunction.

Parsons viewed illness as a form of social deviance and as a social role. The "sick role" exempts one from performing social functions. Therefore, it is acquired by a person from society only in accordance with a specific procedure (by receiving a medical diagnosis and obtaining a sick leave certificate).

6. Holistic Model of Health and Non-communicable (Chronic) Diseases The main theoretical construct of the modern holistic understanding of health became the Biopsychosocial model (BPS), proposed by American physician and psychiatrist George Engel in 1977 (Engel GL. The need for a new medical model: a challenge for biomedicine. Science. 1977 Apr 8;196(4286):129-136. doi: 10.1126/science.847460. PMID: 847460). The model represents an application of a general systems approach to human functioning at all levels of organization: biological, personal-psychological, and also at the socio-psychological level, where social connections with people in the immediate social environment are realized, and further, at the social level — through the individual's inclusion in various institutions of society as a whole.

At the same time, health consists in the "coherence" of human behavior at all these behavioral levels, in the "dynamic unity" of all elements of behavior, and illness can appear at any of them and spread to the others. From this point of view, the biomedical model implies the emergence and development of illness only "from bottom up" and only to the "individual" level; it ignores the psychological and social levels of behavior. Thus, with the change in ideas about causality in medical science, there is a transition from bio-reductionism to a holistic approach: doctors begin to recognize and take into account behavioral causes of diseases.

Biopsychosocial Model (BPS)

Society

Communities, Social Institutions, Organizations

An example of disease development "from top down," according to this model. Sharp social changes, such as those that occurred in Russia's recent history with the collapse of the USSR, led to a new socio-economic situation to which many people could not adapt. One result of these changes was the breakdown of familiar connections in small groups. This fact was acutely experienced by many at the personal level in the form of emotional dysregulation. Then a weak spot appears in the organism, most often the cardiovascular system suffers. A lack of circulation arises, protein deposits occur on cell walls at the tissue level, and as a consequence, a heart attack can occur. In this example, there is no specific factor, but rather a complex of causes that led to the disorganization of the organism and psyche as a whole.

The reverse situation, "from bottom up," is also possible, when dysfunction arises at the cellular or genetic level. This then affects the functioning of body organs, the psyche, and ultimately, a person's behavior in their social environment. And if this is an influential person in society, for example, an organizational leader, their illness, initially appearing at the cellular level, can ultimately affect the lives of a large collective.

Thus, by the end of the 20th century, health ceased to be merely a biological phenomenon reduced to the absence of symptoms. A positive concept of health implies that health is not limited to the absence of diseases, but that health is the presence of certain systemic properties that determine human well-being. Moreover, health is considered not only at the level of the physical body, but also at the level of the person as an individual and at the level of the community in which they live.

7. Some Conclusions in the Context of Prevention Each of us is familiar with thoughts about organizing a healthier diet, or starting to run in the mornings, or eating less sweets, or drinking less coffee or alcohol. But healthy eating is not as simple as stopping by a cafe on the way or boiling dumplings. And to give up excess coffee, sweets, or alcohol, one must learn to derive pleasure in some healthier way. Perhaps this will even require changing one's lifestyle. In other words, we are all, to some extent, concerned with changing our behavior from habitual to more complex. Intellectually, we understand that this is necessary for us. But something is missing for us to change our behavior. This "something" is the main subject of study in health psychology, and its goal is to help people change their behavior in favor of more health-preserving or safe practices.

As mentioned above, a non-communicable disease can be the result of many factors: on the one hand – the circumstances in which a person finds themselves, and on the other hand – the person's internal resources to resist negative circumstances. All these internal and external factors, simultaneously affecting health, have received a special name in behavioral sciences – stress, which has come to be considered the main predictor not only of chronic diseases, but also of all types of behavior that violate certain social norms. Accordingly, reducing stress levels has become the main goal of preventing chronic diseases and all types of behavioral disorders.

The above remark not only reflects the scientific views discussed in this course on the decisive contribution of psychological well-being to a person's health, but also emphasizes that a person cannot be forced to be healthy, but their own natural aspiration towards it can be developed and supported.

At the same time, the question arises: if health is associated with the concept of happiness for us, then why do we have to discuss preventive programs whose purpose is to encourage people to adopt a healthy lifestyle? Why are people not always and in everything inclined to exhibit healthy behavior? Why is it so paradoxically difficult for us to regularly undergo medical examinations, follow doctors' recommendations, exercise, eat properly, abstain from alcohol and tobacco, tear ourselves away from the TV or computer, go to bed on time, observe all personal hygiene requirements, restrain aggression in conflicts, avoid violence, not worry, rationally overcome various stressful situations, be able to relax, and, ultimately, be happy?

The paradox lies in the fact that we must exert effort, expend energy, and experience a certain discomfort to gain some benefits in the distant future. The problem with health-preserving behavior is that the reward for it may come to a person not just too late (years later), but simply in the form of the "non-occurrence" of any disorder (e.g., absence of breast cancer, circulatory system diseases). Such a delayed effect is very difficult to reinforce. It's not easy to refuse a delicious piece of cake at twenty, which guarantees immediate pleasure and only a delayed possibility of avoiding heart problems due to elevated blood cholesterol levels in the distant future. Given that health-preserving behavior often has negative motivation, developing effective preventive health programs is a challenging task for specialists.

Health is not only a highly complex object for scientific description but also a specific mode of behavior requiring constant mobilization of all intellectual and emotional-volitional human resources. To be healthy means to exert effort, to plan, to expend energy, to experience a certain discomfort in order to gain some benefits in the distant future. However, at the same time, a quick and simple feeling of pleasure or emotional relief can be obtained immediately – from a delicious cake, from overeating, from aimlessly flipping through TV channels, from alcohol, from laziness, from aggression or self-aggression, and generally from any behavior that helps reduce emotional tension, as it "simplifies" our perception of a stressful situation.

Nature itself provides us with the motivation for self-effort and choosing healthy behavior through the reinforcement of a feeling of happiness derived from complex activities that increase chances of survival and gene transmission to future generations. This motivation is the main resource for health prevention programs. Metaphorically, it can be said that the essence of preventive programs lies in influencing a person's choice towards "complex" ways of deriving pleasure from life.

By health, we mean the most highly organized behavior a person is capable of, not only compliance with medical norms, but also a subjective sense of well-being, successful social functioning, and the state of public institutions, organizations, and social groups in which that person is included. And considering that today people have the highest life expectancy and the highest level of health in all of human history, we can assume that health standards will continue to rise, and human behavior will become increasingly highly organized, and no one knows the theoretical limits of this growth.
